cells.tense: You are here, and the pen is in your hand where you stand.
cells.ask: Put something you gave lately alongside something you got, both on the page, and leave the pair sitting there for a day without straightening either.
cells.core:
You can feel when a trade between two people has gone lopsided before anyone says it. One of you is owed and it comes back as owing, and the exchange levels itself without a scene. That part works. The pattern reaches you with nothing attached, so you see what's fair and don't have to assemble it.

There's a settled exchange between you now, tilted, and the eye keeps checking whether it will widen. What you were given is in your hands exactly as it came, so keep it that way instead of reworking the arrangement — put what moved each way on the page, set the pen down, and don't touch it. Whatever is still uneven gets to sit while you look, and the fairness has room to show itself.
cells.sheetLine: You watch a tilt in an exchange that's already sitting level.
cells.verb: giving and receiving brought back level between people
cells.place: where the pattern is seen with nothing hanging off it

cells.tense: You are bracing for an exchange that hasn't happened yet, somewhere ahead of you.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: Ask the other person what their half is before you settle anything. Then do yours, and leave theirs where it sits.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is a settling of accounts, and you're carrying both people's ledgers before anyone has spoken. Every possible tilt gets worked through in advance, so nothing can catch you out. A reading that used to flow now runs through a tally, and a trade stops being between people when one person does both sides of the arithmetic.

Persistence here isn't gripping harder; it's holding your own half and letting the other half stay with its owner. Put your half in the open once to the person you're squared up with, then do your part and stop there. Their side holds without your help, and you can tell because a load that isn't yours comes off when you set it down.

cells.tense: You were at that door once, and you are standing at it again.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Take a settlement you keep replaying. Write two lines — what was given, what came back — and add nothing else to them.
cells.core:
A reckoning did not finish, and the door on it stayed where it was. Since then, keeping your hands still has been easier than settling anything, and being owed has sat more comfortably than owing. What's fair stays a question you leave open, and the quiet around it has begun to look like an answer.

Going back out there won't be forced. Pick a settling you keep turning over and sharpen one line through it — what was handed over, what came back, two facts written down and nothing added. The distinction is thin and it belongs to you, and once it exists the account has a shape. You'll see what you're looking at, and the door has somewhere to move.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and the page you're on is already written on.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: When fairness between two people is sitting with you, keep your read of it for an hour before saying it.
cells.core:
You watch exchanges between people level and tilt again, and before anyone says what's owed you've already read it. Something in you lands on a situation between two people, and you file that as noticing. Then the balance gets adjusted, quietly, and the story you keep is that it corrected itself.

Reading a picture like that was not the hard part. The hard part is that your read has been coming out looking like the room's, not yours. When you see what's owed between people, wait an hour before saying it — hold both sides where you can see them while the other person arrives there too. What you saw was yours, and it keeps for an hour.

attempts.check: The record does not say whether the person names the pattern they keep seeing to the people living inside it; the whole Balanced cell rests on that being possible. A reader could reasonably say they do say it and just don't call it anything — the ask survives that, since the pause before the conclusion is still one act and one sentence, and costs nothing. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'held in one hand' figure in the last cell — a picture I'd enjoy writing; I've pulled it back to something they'd recognise themselves. The other risk is praise: 'you read the water's direction from no clue at all' — I've kept it to what the capacity does in a moment a person could point at.
